newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia sees PNG crisis boosting Bougainville peace.
newsitem.headline: Australia sees PNG crisis boosting Bougainville peace.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's caretaker government has the perfect opportunity to find a peaceful end to the nine-year secessionist rebellion on Bougainville island, a senior Australian official said on Wednesday.

The foreign affairs department official, who asked not to be named, said the Australian government hoped PNG's caretaker prime minister John Giheno would seize the opportunity to initiate a Bougainville peace plan and a possible ceasefire.

"If the government of PNG signs on to a peace strategy, which is one of its options in the present situation ... it seems to me that this is a golden opportunity and it's one that I think should be seized and would be a bit tragic if it wasn't," the official told reporters.
Plans to use mercenaries to quell the Bougainville rebellion sparked PNG's worst crisis in 22 years of independence and caused Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan to step aside last week.

Chan also instigated a public inquiry into the planned use of about 70 foreign mercenaries, who were expelled from PNG before they could launch an assault on Bougainville to crush the uprising and recapture the vast Panguna copper mine.
"We've seen what a cancer Bougainville is for PNG, we've seen the extremes that some people have felt it necessary to go to to come to grips with it," the Australian official said.

"Surely, in the situation, you've got an opportunity where the mercenaries have been dismissed, there's a peace strategy that could be endorsed and promoted, there's an opportunity to declare a ceasefire.
"I would have thought, seen from the distance and comfort of Canberra, that you could really seek to push forward on this process."
PNG has failed to solve the Bougainville ethnic uprising despite 13 rounds of peace talks, numerous military offensives and billions of dollars in military costs.
The conflict has already left thousands dead, either from fighting or a lack of medical facilities on the blockaded island some 800 km (500 miles) north-east of PNG capital Port Moresby.

The latest crisis erupted when PNG army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok called for Chan to resign over the $36 million contract with British mercenary firm Sandline International. Singirok said the mercenaries would cause the deaths of many civilians without bringing peace any closer.
Singirok was promptly sacked, but remained the focal point for 10 days of anti-Chan protests.

Last Wednesday, Chan told parliament he, along with deputy Chris Haiveta and Defence Minister Mathias Ijape, would step aside during the inquiry. The inquiry began on Tuesday and is due to last until April 18.
